intro.t: A troubled church, addressed point by point.
b: Paul founded the church in Corinth around AD 50. A few years later it was divided into fan clubs, proud of its gifts, careless about sex and money, suing its own members, and treating the Lord’s Supper as a private dinner party. Paul answers the reports and questions one by one. Again and again he brings each issue back to the cross, the Spirit, and love.

Out of these corrections come some of the best-known passages in the Bible: the wisdom of the cross (chapters 1–2), the body as the Spirit’s temple (chapter 6), the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper (chapter 11), love (chapter 13), and the resurrection (chapter 15).

Corinth stood on the narrow neck of land joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a harbour on each side: Lechaeum to the west and Cenchreae to the east. Goods and even small ships were hauled across the isthmus on a paved trackway, so the city grew rich on trade. The old Greek city was destroyed by the Roman general Mummius in 146 BC and lay almost empty for a century. Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, settled largely by freed slaves and army veterans. By Paul’s time it was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia: new, wealthy, ambitious and very mixed.

Excavations since 1896 (mainly by the American School of Classical Studies at Athens) have uncovered the forum, the speaker’s platform (bēma) where Paul probably stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12), the meat market (macellum, compare 10:25), a theatre seating about 14,000, many temples, and a broken doorway inscription reading ‘[Syna]gogue of the Hebr[ews]’. At the temple of the healing god Asclepius, excavators found many clay models of body parts left as offerings for healing. Some scholars think Paul’s picture of the church as a body with many parts (12:12–27) would have struck Corinthians who knew those offerings.

The famous reputation. Corinth’s immorality was already proverbial in the time of the Athenian comic poet Aristophanes (5th century BC). The Greek geographer Strabo wrote that the temple of Aphrodite once had more than a thousand temple prostitutes. Many scholars now regard that figure as unreliable, since it describes the old Greek city, not Paul’s Roman one, and may reflect Athenian slander. But the letter itself shows that sexual sin was a real problem in the church (5:1; 6:12–20).

hist.t: Dating Paul’s visit: the Gallio inscription
b: An inscription found at Delphi, part of a letter from the emperor Claudius, names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia. It places Gallio’s term of office around AD 51–52 (some date it a year later). Paul was brought before Gallio during his 18-month stay in Corinth (Acts 18:11–12). This is one of the few fixed dates in the New Testament, and most dates for Paul’s life are worked out from it. Paul probably arrived in Corinth about AD 50 and left in 51 or 52.
Gallio himself is well known. He was the brother of the philosopher Seneca, Nero’s tutor, and like his brother he later took his own life under Nero.

b: Paul’s authorship is not seriously disputed. He wrote from Ephesus (16:8) in about AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. He had already written them an earlier letter that is now lost (5:9). He was answering a report from ‘Chloe’s household’ (1:11) and a letter the church had sent him (7:1), probably carried by Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus (16:17).

The letter was valued very early. Around AD 95 the church in Rome wrote to Corinth (the letter called 1 Clement), saying: ‘Take up the epistle of the blessed Apostle Paul’, and reminding them that he had written about Cephas, Apollos and their factions. It is quoted by Ignatius and Polycarp early in the 2nd century, and it is in every early list of New Testament books. The oldest surviving copy, in the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), contains almost the whole letter.
Some scholars in the 20th century suggested that 1 Corinthians was stitched together from several shorter letters, but they could not agree on how, and most scholars now read it as a single letter.

1.t: Factions named after leaders — and Paul's response is to be glad he baptised almost nobody, which tells you how seriously he took the personality cult.
The cross as scandal to Jews and nonsense to Greeks. God chose the weak and the low to nullify the things that are, so that nobody boasts before him.

2.t: Paul compares the Spirit to a person's own spirit, knowing what is within — and says we have the mind of Christ. A key passage on how Scripture is understood.

3.t: Work tested by fire; some survives, some burns, and the builder is saved either way. The passage is about ministry, not salvation.

5.t: A case of incest the congregation is proud of tolerating. Paul's instruction is severe, and 2 Corinthians 2 shows it was aimed at restoration. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

6.t: A list of those who will not inherit the kingdom, followed immediately by the past tense. The verse is quoted far more often for its first half than its second.

7.t: Paul answers questions they sent. He treats singleness as a genuine good rather than a waiting room, which was unusual then and is unusual now.

9.t: Adaptation in method, never in message — Paul says this within a chapter about surrendering rights.

10.t: Two promises: it is common, and there is a way out. Neither says the pressure will be removed.

11.h: The Supper, received and handed on
11.t: The earliest written account of the Lord's Supper, predating the Gospels. Paul says he received it from the Lord.

Christians have divided over this for five hundred years. Roman Catholics hold the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; Lutherans that he is present in and with them; the Reformed that he is truly present to faith by the Spirit though the elements do not change; and many evangelicals that it is chiefly a memorial. We stand with the Reformed view, and we would not refuse the table to a brother holding any of the others. What nobody disputes is that Jesus commanded it and that it proclaims his death until he comes. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

12.t: Gifts differ, the Spirit does not. Verse 11 says the Spirit distributes to each one as he wills, which is a statement about a person rather than a power.

This is a live disagreement among evangelicals and within Reformed churches. Cessationists hold that the revelatory and sign gifts ceased with the apostles; continuationists that the Spirit still gives them, while insisting everything be tested by Scripture. Both are held by serious people. What Paul actually argues in this chapter is not about timing at all: the gifts differ, the Spirit does not, and they exist for the common good rather than for display. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

13.t: Written as a correction to a congregation obsessed with the spectacular, not as a wedding reading. Its position between two chapters on gifts is the argument.

15.t: Verses 3 to 5 are a formula Paul received and passed on, dating within a few years of the crucifixion. It is the single most important piece of evidence for the early belief in the resurrection.

15.h: If Christ has not been raised
15.t: Paul stakes everything on a historical claim and says that if it is false, Christians are to be pitied. He does not offer a fallback.
Not a ghost and not the same body unchanged — sown perishable, raised imperishable. The chapter ends in the only place it could: therefore stand firm.

16.t: An Aramaic prayer — our Lord, come — preserved in a Greek letter. Evidence that the earliest Aramaic-speaking Christians prayed directly to Jesus.

4.t: Paul refuses to be judged by the Corinthians, and then says he does not even judge himself. The verdict that matters comes later and from elsewhere.
Heavy irony. Paul contrasts their self-satisfaction with the apostles' actual conditions: hungry, beaten, homeless, treated as the world's rubbish.

8.t: On food offered to idols. Paul agrees with the strong on the facts and then subordinates the point to love for the weaker brother.
Paul takes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4 and distributes its two terms — God and Lord — between the Father and Jesus, inside an argument for monotheism.

14.t: Paul's consistent criterion is whether the church is built up. Five intelligible words are worth more than ten thousand nobody understands.

Everything in a fitting and orderly way, because God is not a God of disorder. The passage on women speaking is among the most disputed in Paul, and the honest position is that its scope is contested. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

14.h: The hardest verses in the chapter
14.t: Paul's instruction about women being silent is genuinely difficult, partly because he has already assumed in chapter 11 that women pray and prophesy in the gathering. Readings include a restriction on judging prophecy, on disruptive questioning, or on the authoritative teaching office. Anyone who tells you this is simple has not read it carefully. Whatever its scope, it sits inside a chapter whose stated aim is order and the building up of the church. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

1.ctx: Paul writes from Ephesus, about AD 53–55, to the church he had founded a few years earlier. Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader in Corinth who was beaten in front of Gallio (Acts 18:17), now a believer and with Paul, though we cannot be sure.
1.mean: Paul calls himself ‘called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God’. That matters, because some in Corinth were questioning his authority (chapters 4 and 9). He writes ‘To the church of God in Corinth’: the church belongs to God, not to Corinth and not to any leader. Its members are ‘sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy’. Holiness is first something God has given them (they are set apart as his) and then something they must live out. Paul also reminds them they belong with ‘all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ’. Corinth is not the only church in the world.
1.big: A church full of problems is still God’s holy people, and must start living like it.
1.diff: Calling on the name. ‘Call on the name of the LORD’ is Old Testament language for worshipping the one God (Joel 2:32). Paul applies it, without explanation, to Jesus. Little more than twenty years after the crucifixion, Jewish believers like Paul were calling on Jesus as Lord.

1.ctx: Ancient letters usually opened with a thanksgiving. Paul’s thanksgivings often hint at the themes to come.
1.mean: Paul thanks God for the grace given them. They have been ‘enriched in every way, in all speech and all knowledge’ and ‘do not lack any spiritual gift’. These are the very things the Corinthians were proud of, and which Paul will later correct (chapters 12–14). But he thanks God for them first, because they are gifts. The confidence for the future rests on God, not on them: ‘He will sustain you to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.’ ‘God, who has called you into fellowship with His Son Jesus Christ our Lord, is faithful.’
1.big: God’s faithfulness, not the church’s performance, guarantees that he will finish what he began.

1.ctx: The first problem Paul tackles. Greek cities admired public speakers and teachers, and students took pride in which famous teacher they followed. Apollos was an eloquent Jewish teacher from Alexandria who had worked in Corinth after Paul (Acts 18:24–19:1). Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.
1.mean: Some of ‘Chloe’s household’ had told Paul about quarrels. People were saying, ‘I follow Paul,’ ‘I follow Apollos,’ ‘I follow Cephas,’ or ‘I follow Christ.’ Even the last group was using Christ as a party badge. Paul’s answer is three blunt questions: ‘Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptized into the name of Paul?’ He is relieved he baptised so few of them. He is not belittling baptism; he wants no one to think they were joined to him rather than to Christ. His calling was ‘to preach the gospel, not with words of wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power’.
1.big: Loyalty to human leaders divides the church, which belongs to Christ alone.

1.ctx: Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. Preaching a crucified man as Lord sounded absurd to Greeks and offensive to Jews, who read Deuteronomy 21:23 as putting a hanged man under God’s curse.
1.mean: ‘The message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.’ Quoting Isaiah 29:14, Paul says God has turned the world’s wisdom upside down: ‘the world through its wisdom did not know Him’, so God chose to save people through a message that sounds foolish. ‘Jews demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles’. To those God calls, the crucified Christ is ‘the power of God and the wisdom of God’.
1.big: The cross looks like weakness and foolishness, but it is God’s power and wisdom for salvation.

1.ctx: Paul points to the Corinthian church itself as evidence. Most members were ordinary people: workers, freed slaves and slaves. A few, like Crispus, Gaius and Erastus, were people of some standing.
1.mean: ‘Not many of you were wise by human standards; not many were powerful; not many were of noble birth.’ God deliberately ‘chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise’, and the weak, lowly and despised, ‘so that no one may boast in His presence.’ Their salvation was God’s doing: ‘It is because of Him that you are in Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption.’ So the only boasting left is the kind Jeremiah 9:24 allows: ‘Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.’
1.big: God chooses the unimpressive so that all glory goes to him and all boasting is in Christ.
1.diff: ‘God chose’. Reformed readers see here God’s free choice of whom he will save: the Corinthians are in Christ ‘because of Him’, not because they were wiser or better than others (compare Westminster Confession 3). Arminian (Wesleyan) readers agree that salvation is entirely God’s gift and leaves no room for boasting, but take ‘chose’ here to describe the kind of people God delights to save, rather than a fixed decision about particular individuals. Both agree on Paul’s point: the church is made up of people God has rescued, not people who impressed him.

2.h: Paul’s Message by the Spirit’s Power
2.ctx: Travelling speakers in Corinth were judged on their delivery, looks and polish. Paul had arrived from Athens, where few had believed (Acts 17:32–34).
2.mean: Paul deliberately did not try to impress. ‘I resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.’ He came ‘in weakness and fear, and with much trembling’. Yet people believed, because his preaching came ‘with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that your faith would not rest on men’s wisdom, but on God’s power.’ This is not a rejection of careful thought; Paul argues carefully all through this letter. It is a refusal to make the speaker, rather than Christ, the attraction.
2.big: Faith that rests on God’s power, not on persuasive technique, is the kind that lasts.

2.ctx: Having rejected the world’s wisdom, Paul says there is a true wisdom. Some Corinthians thought of themselves as the ‘spiritual’ elite; Paul turns their own words back on them.
2.mean: There is a ‘mysterious and hidden wisdom of God’, planned ‘before time began’. The powerful did not grasp it: ‘if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.’ It cannot be discovered by human cleverness (‘No eye has seen, no ear has heard’), but ‘God has revealed it to us by the Spirit.’ Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts, as only a man’s own spirit knows his. ‘The natural man does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned.’ Believers, by contrast, ‘have the mind of Christ.’
2.big: God’s wisdom is grasped only as his Spirit opens our understanding.
2.diff: The ‘natural man’ (verse 14). Reformed theology reads this as showing that, without the Spirit’s new birth, no one can truly receive the gospel; the Spirit must first open the heart. Arminian (Wesleyan) theology agrees that no one can come to God unaided, but teaches that God’s ‘prevenient’ grace (grace that goes before) is at work in everyone, enabling them to respond. Both reject the idea that people find God by their own intelligence. ‘The Lord of glory’ (verse 8) echoes Old Testament language for God (compare ‘the King of glory’ in Psalm 24:7–10), here given to the crucified Jesus.

3.ctx: Paul returns to the factions of chapter 1. The Corinthians thought themselves spiritually advanced; Paul says the opposite.
3.mean: ‘I could not address you as spiritual, but as worldly—as infants in Christ.’ The proof is their ‘jealousy and dissension’. Rivalry between fan clubs is just ordinary human behaviour. As for the leaders they are fighting over: ‘What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? They are servants through whom you believed’. ‘I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.’ The workers are ‘one in purpose’ and each will be rewarded for his own work. The church belongs to neither: ‘you are God’s field, God’s building.’
3.big: Leaders are only servants; God alone gives growth.

3.ctx: Paul develops the building picture. Corinth’s own history gave it force: the city had been sacked and burned in 146 BC, and was probably rebuilt partly from the stone and metal that survived.
3.mean: Paul laid the foundation ‘as an expert builder’, and others are building on it. ‘No one can lay a foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.’ What is built on it may be durable (‘gold, silver, precious stones’) or flimsy (‘wood, hay, or straw’). On the Day of judgement, ‘the fire will prove the quality of each man’s work.’ Work that survives will be rewarded. If it burns, the builder ‘will suffer loss. He himself will be saved, but only as if through the flames.’ Like a man escaping a burning house he built badly, he is rescued, but his work is lost.
3.big: Everything must be built on Christ, and each person’s work will be tested by God.
3.diff: Who is in view? Many commentators (including Calvin, who says ‘Paul assuredly speaks of ministers alone’) think Paul is speaking first of church leaders and teachers. Others apply it to every believer’s life’s work. Purgatory? Catholic teaching cites this verse among others when it speaks of a purification after death for those who die in God’s grace but still need cleansing: ‘the tradition of the Church, by reference to certain texts of Scripture, speaks of a cleansing fire’ (Catechism 1031). Protestants read the fire as the testing of each person’s work on the Day of judgement, not a cleansing of the soul after death. Calvin called purgatory ‘silly trifles’; Wesley said this text ‘utterly overthrows’ it. They point out that the fire tests works, not souls, and that it comes on ‘the Day’ of Christ’s return rather than at each person’s death. Many modern commentators of different traditions likewise read the passage as about the final judgement of believers’ work. All agree that the one who is saved is saved by Christ, the foundation, not by the quality of his work.

3.ctx: Corinth had many temples. Destroying or defiling a temple was treated as a serious crime by Jews and Gentiles alike.
3.mean: ‘Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?’ The ‘you’ is plural: the church together is where God now lives. So: ‘If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him’. Splitting the church is not a minor matter. Paul then deflates the pride behind the factions. The world’s wisdom is foolishness to God, so ‘stop boasting in men.’ It is backwards to say ‘I follow Paul’ (1:12), because the truth is the other way round: ‘All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future… and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.’
3.big: The church is God’s temple, and those who divide it answer to God.
3.diff: Here the temple is the church as a whole. In 6:19 Paul applies the same picture to each believer’s body.

4.ctx: The Corinthians were ranking their teachers. Paul answers with some of his sharpest irony.
4.mean: Apostles are ‘servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God’, and ‘it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.’ So Paul is not troubled by their verdicts on him, or even his own: ‘It is the Lord who judges me.’ ‘Therefore judge nothing before the appointed time’. Then a question that undercuts all pride: ‘What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?’ The Corinthians act as if they had already arrived: ‘Already you have become rich. Without us, you have become kings.’ By contrast the apostles are like condemned prisoners at the end of a procession, ‘a spectacle to the whole world’, hungry, homeless, ‘the scum of the earth’.
4.big: Christian leaders answer to the Lord, and everything we have is a gift, so there is no room for pride.

b: Corinth had a large theatre, seating about 14,000, and some scholars (such as Jerome Murphy-O’Connor) suggest Paul had public spectacles like those in mind when he wrote that the apostles had become ‘a spectacle to the whole world’ (verse 9). It is a reasonable suggestion, but Paul does not say so.

4.ctx: A change of tone, from irony to appeal. A ‘guardian’ (Greek paidagōgos) was a household slave who took children to school and kept them in line; he was not their father.
4.mean: ‘I am not writing this to shame you, but to warn you as my beloved children.’ They may have ‘ten thousand guardians in Christ’, but only one father: ‘in Christ Jesus I became your father through the gospel.’ So ‘I urge you to imitate me.’ He is sending Timothy to remind them how he lives, which is ‘exactly what I teach everywhere in every church.’ Some have grown arrogant, thinking Paul will not come back. He will, and ‘the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power.’ ‘Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love and with a gentle spirit?’
4.big: Paul corrects the church as a father who brought them to faith, and he expects to be imitated.

5.ctx: A case the church was tolerating. The law of Moses forbade a man to have sexual relations with his father’s wife (Leviticus 18:8), and Paul says even pagans would not accept it.
5.mean: ‘A man has his father’s wife’, a kind of immorality ‘intolerable even among pagans’. Worse, the church was proud of its tolerance, perhaps as proof of its freedom. They should have grieved and ‘removed from your fellowship the man who did this’. When they meet, with Paul present in spirit and ‘the power of the Lord Jesus’, they are to ‘hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.’ The aim is rescue, not revenge. Sin left alone spreads: ‘a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough’. As Israel cleared out yeast at Passover, so they must clear out sin, ‘For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.’
5.big: Tolerating open, unrepentant sin harms the whole church; discipline aims at the sinner’s rescue.
5.diff: ‘Hand this man over to Satan’. Most take this to mean putting him out of the church’s fellowship into the world, ‘Satan’s territory’, where he will feel the full weight of his sin and, it is hoped, repent. ‘The destruction of the flesh’ is read either as the destruction of his sinful nature, or as physical suffering (compare 11:30). 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 may describe a repentant offender being welcomed back, though whether it is the same man is debated. Churches differ in how formal discipline is carried out, but almost all agree it must be done carefully, through proper leadership, and with restoration as the goal.

5.ctx: Paul had written to them before (verse 9). That earlier letter is lost, and they had misunderstood it.
5.mean: ‘I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.’ He did not mean people outside the church; ‘In that case you would have to leave this world.’ He meant ‘anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. 6.ctx: Lawsuits were heard in public, in the civic courts. Verses 7–8 show that some members were using them to cheat fellow believers.
6.mean: ‘If any of you has a grievance against another, how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!’ If believers will one day share in judging the world and even angels, they can surely settle everyday disputes. ‘Is there really no one among you wise enough to arbitrate between his brothers?’ Suing one another at all is already a defeat. ‘Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?’ Instead they are the ones doing the cheating, ‘even against your own brothers!’
6.big: Believers should settle disputes within the church, even at personal cost, rather than shame Christ in public.
6.diff: Paul is speaking about civil disputes between believers, not about reporting crimes. Romans 13:1–4 says the authorities are God’s servants to punish wrongdoing, and churches today rightly report abuse and other crimes to the police.

6.ctx: Some Corinthians seem to have argued that what they did with their bodies did not matter spiritually. Paul quotes their slogans (‘Everything is permissible for me’; ‘Food for the stomach’) and answers them.
6.mean: ‘Do not be deceived: Neither the sexually immoral, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor men who submit to or perform homosexual acts, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor verbal abusers, nor swindlers, will inherit the kingdom of God.’ Then the turn: ‘And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.’ As for their slogans: ‘not everything is beneficial’, and ‘I will not be mastered by anything.’ ‘The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord’. God will raise our bodies, they are ‘members of Christ’, so uniting them with a prostitute is unthinkable.
6.big: The gospel names sin plainly and transforms sinners: ‘that is what some of you were. But you were washed’.
6.diff: The words in verse 9. The BSB’s ‘men who submit to or perform homosexual acts’ translates two Greek words. Malakos literally means ‘soft’ and was used of men who took the passive role in sex with men. Arsenokoitēs is a rare compound of ‘male’ and ‘bed’ (a word for sexual intercourse). It may have been coined from the Greek translation of Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where the same two words stand side by side. Where scholars stand. Most commentators (for example Fee, Garland, Thiselton) conclude that the two words refer to the passive and active partners in male same-sex intercourse; Garland translates them ‘those males who are penetrated sexually by males’ and ‘those males who sexually penetrate males’. In 1980 the historian John Boswell argued that the words did not condemn homosexual relationships as such. Some scholars since have argued that Paul had in mind only exploitative forms common in his day, such as the sexual use of boys or slaves, or prostitution. Most commentators have not been persuaded, noting that Paul draws on the Leviticus wording, which is general, and on Jewish teaching that rejected all such acts. Churches. Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches teach that sexual intimacy belongs only within marriage between a man and a woman. Some Protestant denominations have changed their teaching in recent decades. The pastoral point. This is one item in a list that also includes greed, drunkenness and abusive speech, and Paul says ‘some of you were’ these things. He is writing to forgiven people. The church is a community of washed sinners, not of people who were never tempted.

7.ctx: Paul turns to the questions the Corinthians had written to him. ‘It is good to abstain from sexual relations’ (verse 1) is probably their slogan, which Paul quotes and then qualifies. Some of them seem to have thought that sex, even within marriage, was unspiritual.
7.mean: Marriage is the right place for sex: ‘each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.’ Within marriage, each has a duty to the other. Strikingly for his time, Paul says it equally of both: ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.’ They may abstain for a time of prayer, by agreement, but must come together again. Paul values singleness, but ‘each man has his own gift from God’. To the married he passes on the Lord’s own command: no divorce. If a believer is married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay, they must not divorce, because the unbelieving spouse and the children are ‘sanctified’ through the believer. ‘But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases.’
7.big: Marriage is good and mutual, and should be kept wherever possible.
7.diff: Deserted by an unbelieving spouse (verse 15). ‘Not bound’ is read in two main ways. Many Protestants take it to mean the deserted believer is free to remarry. The Westminster Confession allows divorce for ‘adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied by the church, or civil magistrate’ (24.6). Others take it to mean only that the believer need not fight to keep the marriage, and should not remarry. Catholic canon law calls this the ‘Pauline privilege’: a marriage between two unbaptised people is dissolved when one is baptised, the other departs, and the baptised person marries again (canon 1143). ‘Your children… are holy’ (verse 14). The word does not mean they are automatically saved, but that they are set apart, belonging within the circle of God’s people. Calvin used this to argue for infant baptism: ‘If the Lord admits them into the Church by his word, why should we refuse them the sign?’ Baptists, who baptise only those who profess faith, reply that the same verse calls the unbelieving husband ‘sanctified’, and no one baptises him on that basis. Practical note. Questions about divorce and remarriage are painful and personal. They are best worked through with a church’s own leaders.

7.ctx: A principle Paul applies to circumcision, slavery and marriage alike. Some Jewish men in the Greek world had surgery to hide their circumcision; some Gentile converts wanted to be circumcised.
7.mean: ‘Each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him.’ Becoming a Christian does not require changing your outward situation. ‘Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts.’ To slaves: ‘Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.’ In Christ the slave is ‘the Lord’s freedman’ and the free man is ‘Christ’s slave’. ‘You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.’
7.big: Christians can serve God where they are, because their calling in Christ matters more than their status.
7.diff: Paul does not approve of slavery here. He tells slaves to take freedom if they can, and his teaching that slave and master are brothers in Christ (Philemon 16) undermined the whole system.

7.ctx: Paul turns to the unmarried, in light of ‘the present crisis’. This may refer to a local hardship such as famine, or to the pressures of the last days in general.
7.mean: Paul gives ‘a judgment’ rather than a command from the Lord. Because of the present crisis, it is good to stay as you are. ‘But if you do marry, you have not sinned.’ ‘The time is short’ and ‘this world in its present form is passing away’, so believers should hold everything loosely: marriage, grief, joy, possessions. The unmarried person can give ‘undivided devotion to the Lord’; the married person rightly gives attention to pleasing their spouse. A widow may remarry, ‘as long as he belongs to the Lord.’
7.big: Both singleness and marriage are good gifts, and singleness offers particular freedom to serve the Lord.
7.diff: Paul’s own judgement. Paul distinguishes the Lord’s command (verse 10) from his own advice (verses 12, 25). Most Christians still treat his advice as inspired Scripture (he adds, ‘I think that I too have the Spirit of God’), but as wise counsel for circumstances rather than a rule binding everyone. Catholic and Orthodox traditions have drawn on this chapter in honouring vowed celibacy. Protestants have emphasised that marriage is honourable and not a lesser calling (Hebrews 13:4).

8.ctx: Little meat was available in Corinth that had not come from animals sacrificed at a temple, and meals were held in temple precincts (verse 10 mentions ‘eating in an idol’s temple’). Refusing every such meal could cost a believer friendships and business.
8.mean: The ‘strong’ Corinthians said, ‘We all have knowledge’: idols are nothing, so eating is harmless. Paul agrees with the theology: ‘an idol is nothing at all in the world’. But ‘Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.’ ‘For us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist.’ Not everyone has this knowledge. A believer with a weak conscience, seeing a stronger Christian ‘eating in an idol’s temple’, may be drawn back into idolatry. ‘So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge.’ ‘Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again’.
8.big: Love for a weaker brother matters more than the freedom that knowledge gives.
8.diff: One God, one Lord (verse 6). Paul takes the Shema, Israel’s confession that ‘the LORD our God, the LORD is One’ (Deuteronomy 6:4), and divides its words between the Father (‘one God’) and Jesus (‘one Lord’). He also names Jesus as the one ‘through whom all things came’, that is, the Creator. This is one of the earliest places where Jesus is included within the identity of the one God, and it may have shaped the Nicene Creed’s confession of ‘one God, the Father Almighty’ and ‘one Lord Jesus Christ’.

9.ctx: Paul uses himself as an example of giving up rights for others, following on from chapter 8. Some in Corinth questioned whether he was a real apostle, partly because he refused their money and worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3).
9.mean: ‘Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?’ The church itself is proof: ‘you are the seal of my apostleship’. Paul has every right to be supported, like soldiers, farmers, shepherds and priests. The Law says so too: ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.’ And ‘the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel.’ ‘But we did not exercise this right. Instead, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.’ Preaching is not optional for him: ‘Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!’ His reward is to offer it ‘free of charge’.
9.big: Paul gave up his own rights so that nothing would hinder the gospel.
9.diff: Paying ministers. This chapter is the main New Testament basis for churches supporting their pastors (compare 1 Timothy 5:17–18). Paul’s own choice to work for a living shows that ministers may also choose not to be paid, when that helps the gospel. The Lord’s brothers (verse 5): see History & setting of James for how different traditions understand them.

9.ctx: Paul’s missionary principle, still within his argument about giving up rights for others.
9.mean: ‘Though I am free of obligation to anyone, I make myself a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible.’ Among Jews he kept Jewish customs; among Gentiles he did not, though he was never ‘outside the law of God but am under the law of Christ’. ‘To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.’
9.big: Paul adapts everything except the gospel itself in order to reach people.
9.diff: ‘All things to all people’ is about cultural flexibility (food, customs, approach), not changing the message or compromising on right and wrong. Paul immediately adds that he is under ‘the law of Christ’.

9.ctx: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games, one of the great athletic festivals of the Greek world. See The Isthmian Games below.
9.mean: ‘Run in such a way as to take the prize.’ Athletes train ‘with strict discipline’ for ‘a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable.’ Paul does not run aimlessly or shadow-box: ‘I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified.’
9.big: The Christian life calls for disciplined, purposeful effort toward a prize that lasts.
9.diff: ‘Disqualified’. Reformed readers generally take this as a real warning that God uses to keep his people persevering; those truly in Christ will heed such warnings and be kept. Some take ‘disqualified’ to mean losing reward or usefulness in ministry, rather than salvation. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers take it to mean that even an apostle could fall away; Wesley glossed it ‘Disapproved by the Judge, and so falling short of the prize.’ All agree Paul took his own spiritual discipline seriously.

b: Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, at the sanctuary of Poseidon near the city. They drew crowds from all over Greece, and one of the city’s leading officials was the president of the games. In Paul’s day the victor’s crown was made of plants, which soon withered. Paul’s ‘crown that is perishable’ (verse 25) would have meant something to every reader.

10.ctx: Some Corinthians seem to have felt safe because they had been baptised and shared the Lord’s Supper. Paul shows that Israel had similar privileges and still fell.
10.mean: Israel’s ancestors were all ‘baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea’, all ate the same spiritual food and drank from ‘the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ.’ ‘Nevertheless, God was not pleased with most of them’. They fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling. ‘These things… were written down as warnings for us’. ‘So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.’ Then encouragement: ‘No temptation has seized you except what is common to man. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear. But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.’
10.big: Privileges do not guarantee faithfulness, but God is faithful to provide a way through every temptation.
10.diff: A misused verse. Verse 13 is often quoted as ‘God won’t give you more than you can handle’. Its subject is temptation to sin, not suffering in general; Paul himself was at times ‘under a burden far beyond our ability to endure’ (2 Corinthians 1:8). ‘That rock was Christ’. Paul sees Christ present with Israel in the wilderness, providing for them, which assumes that Christ existed before he was born as a man.

10.ctx: Paul now rules out sharing in meals that were part of pagan worship.
10.mean: ‘Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.’ ‘Is not the cup of blessing that we bless a participation in the blood of Christ? And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?’ ‘Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body’. Eating at a sacrificial meal joins people to what is worshipped there. Idols themselves are nothing, but ‘the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.’ ‘You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too’.
10.big: Believers share in Christ at his table, and so cannot share in pagan worship.
10.diff: ‘Participation’ (Greek koinōnia, also ‘fellowship’, ‘sharing’) in Christ’s body and blood. All Christians agree the Lord’s Supper is a real sharing in Christ and makes the church one body. They differ on how Christ is present. Wesley called the cup ‘The means of our partaking of those invaluable benefits, which are the purchase of the blood of Christ.’ See the glossary entry ‘Lord’s Supper’ for the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed and memorial views in their own words.

10.ctx: Paul sums up his guidance on disputed matters. ‘Everything is permissible’ was probably a Corinthian slogan, which Paul quotes and qualifies.
10.mean: ‘“Everything is permissible,” but not everything is beneficial.’ ‘No one should seek his own good, but the good of others.’ In practice: ‘Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience’, because ‘The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.’ If an unbeliever invites you to dinner, eat what is served. But if someone points out that the food was offered to idols, do not eat it, for the sake of their conscience. ‘So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God.’
10.big: Christian freedom is used for others’ good and for God’s glory.

b: Paul’s word for ‘meat market’ in verse 25 is makellon, borrowed from the Latin macellum. Excavators at Corinth have identified the city’s meat market. Much of the meat sold there had come from animals sacrificed in the city’s many temples, which is why the question of conscience arose.

11.ctx: In public worship, men and women in Corinth were praying and prophesying. Something about how they covered (or did not cover) their heads was causing offence. See Head coverings in Roman Corinth below.
11.mean: ‘The head of every man is Christ, and the head of the woman is man, and the head of Christ is God.’ So a man who prays or prophesies ‘with his head covered dishonors his head’, and a woman who does so ‘with her head uncovered dishonors her head’. Paul argues from creation: ‘woman from man’, and ‘woman for man’. So ‘a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels.’ Then he balances it: ‘In the Lord, however, woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman. For just as woman came from man, so also man is born of woman. But everything comes from God.’ He appeals to what is fitting and to the practice of all the churches.
11.big: Worship should honour God by respecting the difference between men and women, within their mutual dependence in the Lord.
11.diff: One of the hardest passages in Paul. What ‘head’ means. Some scholars argue the Greek kephalē here means authority (for example Robertson and Plummer; Ciampa and Rosner, who ground it in the order of creation). Others argue it means source or origin, since woman came from man (Fee; Barrett). A third view is ‘pre-eminence’. Calvin took it as authority: the man holds ‘the office of the head in respect of ruling her.’ Complementarians (who hold that men and women are equal but have different roles in marriage and church leadership) generally read ‘authority’; egalitarians (who hold that roles are open to both) generally read ‘source’. Are head coverings for today? A minority of churches (for example some Brethren, Mennonite and Reformed congregations) still ask women to cover their heads in worship. Most churches see the covering as the way that culture expressed a lasting principle. Calvin, who thought the covering right in his day, said ‘the one rule to be observed here is το πρέπον — decorum.’ Because of the angels. No one knows for sure. The commonest view is that angels are present at worship and care that it is fitting. Note that Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in the gathering (verse 5). That shapes how chapter 14:34–35 is read.

b: What the Corinthians were doing is not fully clear, and scholars disagree. For men, Roman religion had a well-known custom: a man leading a sacrifice or prayer pulled his toga up over his head (capite velato, ‘with covered head’). A famous statue of the emperor Augustus (about AD 12–14) shows him like this. Some commentators (for example Ciampa and Rosner) think Paul did not want Christian men to look like pagans at worship. Others (for example Garland) think the issue was a hairstyle rather than a cloth covering, though Garland too connects it with pagan sacrifice. Gordon Fee, after weighing the options, concludes we do not know for certain what Paul had in mind for the men.

For women, Paul plainly regards the head covering as a mark of propriety and modesty. He compares an uncovered head with a shaved one, which he calls shameful (verse 6), and he treats leaving it off as a kind of rebellion. Why some Corinthian women were doing so is not clear.

11.ctx: The early church ate the Lord’s Supper as part of a real meal, usually in a wealthier member’s home. Corinth had great gaps between rich and poor. Some scholars think the poorer members, including slaves, arrived late after work to find the food gone.
11.mean: ‘Your gatherings do more harm than good.’ There are divisions: ‘While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.’ So ‘it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat’, and they ‘humiliate those who have nothing’. Paul reminds them what he ‘received from the Lord’: ‘The Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread, and when He had given thanks, He broke it and said, “This is My body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”’ And the cup: ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood’. ‘For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.’ So eating ‘in an unworthy manner’ is serious. ‘Each one must examine himself’, for whoever eats ‘without recognizing the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.’ The practical answer: ‘when you come together to eat, wait for one another.’
11.big: The Lord’s Supper proclaims Christ’s death, and must be shared in a way that honours all his people.
11.diff: The earliest account. This is the earliest written record of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels, and Paul says he had passed it on to them when he founded the church around AD 50. ‘Without recognizing the body’ (verse 29). Calvin read it as failing to distinguish the Lord’s body ‘as a sacred thing from a profane’, treating the Supper like ordinary food. Many modern commentators think ‘the body’ here also, or mainly, means the church as Christ’s body (compare 10:17; 12:27), since the sin Paul is correcting is despising poorer members. How Christ is present. Christians differ: Catholic and Orthodox teach that the bread and wine are changed into Christ’s body and blood; Lutherans that Christ’s true body and blood are present ‘under the bread and wine’; the Reformed that believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit (Calvin: ‘Christ is not a deceiver, to mock us with empty representations’); and many evangelicals stress remembrance. See the glossary entry ‘Lord’s Supper’. Examine yourself is meant to lead to repentance and coming, not to staying away; the Supper is for sinners who trust Christ.

12.ctx: The Corinthians prized dramatic gifts, especially tongues, as signs of spiritual status. Many had come from pagan religion, where ecstatic speech was also known.
12.mean: The first test of the Spirit’s work is what is said about Jesus: ‘no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.’ ‘There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people.’ ‘Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good.’ Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation. ‘All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines.’
12.big: Every gift comes from the one Spirit, for the good of the whole church, not for status.
12.diff: Spirit, Lord, God. Verses 4–6 name the Spirit, the Lord (Jesus) and God (the Father) side by side as the one source of the gifts, one of the patterns in Paul that the church later expressed in the doctrine of the Trinity. ‘As He determines’ presents the Spirit as a person who decides, not an impersonal force. Do all the gifts continue today? Cessationists, including many Reformed Christians, hold that the miraculous gifts confirmed the apostles’ message and ceased with them. B. B. Warfield argued they were ‘part of the credentials of the Apostles’ and ‘necessarily passed away with’ the apostolic church. Continuationists (including many evangelicals, charismatics and Pentecostals) hold that all the gifts continue until Christ returns. See the glossary entry ‘Spiritual gifts’.

12.ctx: Ancient writers often compared a city or society to a body. Paul uses the picture to honour the members who seem weakest.
12.mean: ‘The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts… So it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.’ No part can say it does not belong, and no part can say to another, ‘I do not need you.’ In fact ‘the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable’, and God gives ‘greater honor to the parts that lacked it’. ‘If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it.’
12.big: Every believer is a needed part of Christ’s body, and all share one another’s sufferings and joys.
12.diff: ‘Baptized… in one Spirit’ (verse 13). Most Protestants and Catholics read this as describing what happens to every believer at conversion and baptism: all are joined to Christ’s body by the Spirit. Pentecostals agree that every believer receives the Spirit at the new birth, but teach a further ‘baptism in the Spirit’, ‘distinct from and subsequent to the experience of the new birth’ (Assemblies of God), drawing mainly on Acts.

12.ctx: Paul applies the body picture to the roles God gives in the church.
12.mean: ‘Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.’ God has appointed ‘first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers’, then other gifts. Tongues, which the Corinthians prized most, comes last. ‘Are all apostles? Are all prophets?… Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret?’ In Greek each question expects the answer ‘No’. ‘But eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now I will show you the most excellent way.’
12.big: God gives different gifts to different people, and no single gift is expected of everyone.
12.diff: ‘Do all speak in tongues?’ The expected answer is no. Many cite this against the Pentecostal teaching that tongues is the necessary first sign of baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals commonly reply that Paul is speaking of the ongoing gift of tongues used in church, which not all have, rather than the initial sign which, they hold, all who are baptised in the Spirit receive. ‘The most excellent way’ introduces chapter 13: love.

13.ctx: Often read at weddings, but written to correct a church proud of its gifts and failing in love. Every phrase in verses 4–7 corrects something the Corinthians were doing.
13.mean: ‘If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal.’ Prophecy, knowledge, faith and even self-sacrifice without love are ‘nothing’. ‘Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs.’ ‘It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never fails.’ The gifts are temporary: ‘we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial passes away.’ ‘Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face.’ ‘And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love.’
13.big: Without love even the greatest gifts are worthless, and love will outlast them all.
13.diff: ‘When the perfect comes’. Most interpreters, across traditions, take this to be Christ’s return, when we will see ‘face to face’. Calvin said the perfection ‘begins, indeed, at death’ but will not be fully seen ‘until the day of judgment’, and that applying the passage to the time in between is a mistake; Wesley put it ‘At death and in the last day.’ Some cessationists have taken ‘the perfect’ to mean the completed New Testament, but many cessationists do not rest their case on this verse. Love here is agapē, love that seeks the other’s good at cost to oneself, as Christ did.

b: Corinth was famous for its bronze, which the Roman writer Pliny said was valued ‘before silver and almost even before gold’. The architect Vitruvius mentions bronze in connection with the acoustics of theatres. Some scholars (such as Jerome Murphy-O’Connor) suggest that Paul’s ‘ringing gong or a clanging cymbal’ (13:1) would have called these to mind for Corinthian readers: loud, impressive and hollow. It is an attractive suggestion but cannot be proved.

14.ctx: Paul applies chapter 13 to the gifts the Corinthians were misusing, especially speaking in tongues in church without interpretation.
14.mean: ‘Earnestly pursue love and eagerly desire spiritual gifts, especially the gift of prophecy.’ Someone speaking in a tongue speaks to God, and ‘no one understands him’; prophecy ‘speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort.’ ‘The one who speaks in a tongue edifies himself, but the one who prophesies edifies the church.’ Paul himself speaks in tongues ‘more than all of you’, yet ‘in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.’ If outsiders hear uninterpreted tongues they will think ‘you are out of your minds’; if they hear prophecy, they may be convicted and say, ‘God is truly among you!’
14.big: What is said aloud in church must be understandable and build others up.
14.diff: What were tongues and prophecy? At Pentecost, tongues were human languages the speakers had not learned (Acts 2:6–11). Some think Corinthian tongues were the same; others think they included non-human speech, the ‘tongues of men and of angels’ (13:1), since ‘no one understands him’. New Testament prophecy is understood by some as Spirit-given speech that must be weighed (14:29), not equal to Scripture; others hold that true prophecy carried God’s authority and belonged to the founding of the church. Do they continue? See the glossary entry ‘Spiritual gifts’. All agree on Paul’s rules: love first, intelligible speech in church, and everything for building others up.

14.ctx: Early Christians met in homes, where many people could take part. Paul gives practical rules to keep the gathering orderly. The BSB footnote notes that ‘Some manuscripts place verses 34–35 after verse 40.’
14.mean: ‘When you come together, everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church.’ Two or three may speak in tongues, in turn, and only with interpretation. Two or three prophets may speak, ‘and the others should weigh carefully what is said.’ ‘The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets’; no one is swept along out of control. ‘For God is not a God of disorder, but of peace’. Then: ‘Women are to be silent in the churches. They are not permitted to speak, but must be in submission, as the law says. If they wish to inquire about something, they are to ask their own husbands at home’. Paul ends: ‘be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner.’
14.big: Worship should be orderly and build others up, because it reflects the God of peace.
14.diff: ‘Women are to be silent’ (verses 34–35). This is hard, because in 11:5 Paul assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in church. Where scholars stand. There is no consensus. The main readings are: (1) a general rule, women are not to speak in the assembly (for example Robertson and Plummer); (2) women are not to take part in the judging of prophecies (verse 29), which would put them in authority over men (for example Kistemaker); (3) Paul is stopping disruptive questioning during worship, perhaps by wives questioning their husbands’ prophecies (for example Thiselton; Ciampa and Rosner); (4) the verses were added to the letter later by a copyist (Fee). The last view rests on the fact that some Western manuscripts put the verses after verse 40. Every surviving manuscript contains them somewhere, and many scholars hold that they are Paul’s. Reformed and Wesleyan voices. Calvin read it as forbidding women to teach in public ‘referring to ordinary service, or where there is a Church in a regularly constituted state’, and allowed that ‘a necessity may occur’. Wesley read it as forbidding women to speak ‘By way of teaching in public assemblies’, unless ‘under an extraordinary impulse of the Spirit’. Today. Churches that do not have women as pastors or elders (complementarian) usually read this with 1 Timothy 2:12 as about authoritative teaching. Churches that do (egalitarian) usually read it as a local problem of disorder. Very few churches today forbid women to speak in church at all, which shows that nearly everyone reads it in light of chapter 11. This is a matter on which faithful Christians differ; it is worth discussing with a church’s own leaders.

15.ctx: Some in Corinth were saying ‘there is no resurrection of the dead’ (verse 12). Greek thought often looked down on the body and hoped for the soul to escape it; a raised body seemed absurd (compare Acts 17:32). Paul starts with what everyone in the church already believed.
15.mean: Paul reminds them of the gospel ‘by which… you are saved’. ‘For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve.’ Then to ‘more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living’, then to James, then to all the apostles, ‘And last of all He appeared to me also’. Paul, once the persecutor, says: ‘by the grace of God I am what I am’. ‘This is what we preach, and this is what you believed.’
15.big: The gospel rests on events in history: Christ’s death for sins, his burial, his resurrection and his appearances to many witnesses.
15.diff: ‘For our sins’ and ‘according to the Scriptures’ probably point especially to Isaiah 53, where the servant suffers for the sins of others. ‘He was buried’ matters: in a Jewish setting, saying someone who was buried was raised meant the body was no longer in the grave. Witnesses. Calvin notes that Paul’s list is not complete: ‘He does not, however, adduce them all, for he makes no mention of women.’ The Gospels say women were the first to see the risen Jesus; why this formal summary leaves them out is not certain.

b: Paul says he ‘received’ and ‘passed on’ this summary (15:3), the technical words for handing on a tradition. The language is not typical of Paul, and it uses Peter’s Aramaic name ‘Cephas’. For these reasons scholars across the spectrum treat verses 3–5 (or 3–7) as a creed Paul was taught, not something he composed.

When did he receive it? Paul visited Peter and James in Jerusalem about three years after his conversion (Galatians 1:18–19), and his conversion was within a few years of the crucifixion. As Kirk MacGregor notes in a survey of the scholarship, virtually all critical scholars agree that Paul received it within about five years of the crucifixion, and many date it earlier. This is not only a believing view. The sceptical scholar Gerd Lüdemann wrote that ‘all the elements in the tradition are to be dated to the first two years after the crucifixion’. Scholars disagree on what lay behind the appearances, but most agree that the claim that Jesus had been raised and had appeared to named people was being taught within a very few years of his death, not developed decades later as legend.
Paul adds that most of the more than 500 witnesses were ‘still living’ when he wrote (15:6): in effect, ‘go and ask them’.

15.ctx: The Corinthian doubters seem to have accepted that Jesus rose, but denied that believers’ bodies would be raised.
15.mean: Paul follows their view to its end. ‘If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.’ The apostles would be ‘false witnesses about God’. ‘And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.’ Those who have died in Christ would be lost. ‘If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.’
15.big: Christianity stands or falls on the bodily resurrection of Jesus.
15.diff: Paul does not treat the resurrection as a symbol or a spiritual experience. He says that if it did not happen, Christian faith is false and pointless. This is one reason the evidence matters (see An early creed in the previous note).

15.ctx: ‘Firstfruits’ were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as the pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11).
15.mean: ‘But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.’ ‘For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.’ There is an order: ‘Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him.’ Then the end, when Christ ‘hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power.’ ‘The last enemy to be destroyed is death.’ Finally ‘the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.’ Paul adds an argument from practice: why are some ‘baptized for the dead’, and why does he risk death daily, if the dead are not raised? Without resurrection, ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.’ ‘Bad company corrupts good character’, he warns, probably quoting the Greek playwright Menander.
15.big: Christ’s resurrection is the first of the harvest, guaranteeing the resurrection of all who belong to him.
15.diff: The Son made subject (verse 28). In the 4th century the Arians used this verse to argue that the Son is less than the Father. The historic churches answer that it concerns the Son’s work as the incarnate mediator, not his divine nature. Calvin: Christ ‘is inferior to God, in respect of his human nature’, yet is ‘of one essence with him, and is therefore himself God’; the handing over of the kingdom ends his work as mediator, not his deity. ‘Baptized for the dead’ (verse 29). No one knows for certain what Paul meant, and there are dozens of proposals. (1) Some Corinthians were being baptised on behalf of believers who had died unbaptised (Conzelmann and others). Paul mentions it without approving it, simply to show they believed in the resurrection. (2) People were being baptised ‘because of’ the dead, moved by the hope of rejoining believers who had died (Ciampa and Rosner). (3) Calvin thought it meant people seeking baptism when they were dying, ‘who are looked upon as already dead’; he could not ‘by any means be persuaded’ that proxy baptism was meant. Wesley: ‘Perhaps baptized in hope of blessings to be received after they are numbered with the dead.’ (4) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, citing this verse. The mainstream churches have not practised it, because elsewhere the New Testament ties baptism to each person’s own repentance and faith (Acts 2:38), and because one obscure verse is a weak basis for a practice found nowhere else in Scripture.

15.ctx: The doubters’ question was practical: what could a raised body be like, once the old one has rotted?
15.mean: ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?’ Paul answers with a seed: ‘What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.’ The plant is continuous with the seed, yet far more glorious. God already makes many kinds of bodies, earthly and heavenly. ‘So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.’ Adam, ‘of the dust of the earth’, became a living being; Christ, ‘the last Adam’, is ‘a life-giving spirit’. ‘And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.’
15.big: The resurrection body is continuous with the present one but transformed, as a plant is from its seed.
15.diff: ‘Spiritual body’ does not mean a body made of spirit, or no body at all. Paul’s word means a body fully given life and governed by the Holy Spirit, as ‘natural’ means a body animated by ordinary human life. The risen Jesus could be touched and ate food (Luke 24:39–43). The Westminster Confession says the dead will be raised ‘with the selfsame bodies, and none other’ (32.2), though changed.

15.h: Where, O Death, Is Your Victory?
15.ctx: The climax of the chapter, looking to Christ’s return.
15.mean: ‘Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God’, so we must be changed. ‘Listen, I tell you a mystery: We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet.’ The dead will be raised imperishable, and those still living will be transformed. Then Isaiah 25:8 and Hosea 13:14 will come true: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory.’ ‘Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?’ ‘The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!’ So: ‘be steadfast and immovable. Always excel in the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain.’
15.big: Christ’s victory over death means that nothing done for him is ever wasted.
15.diff: ‘Flesh and blood’ means human nature in its present, mortal state, not bodies as such; the whole chapter insists on a bodily resurrection. Paul expects some believers to be alive when Christ returns (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:15–17), but does not say when that will be.

16.ctx: Paul was collecting money from Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem, a project he cared about deeply (Romans 15:25–27; 2 Corinthians 8–9).
16.mean: ‘On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed.’ The church will choose trusted people to carry the gift to Jerusalem, with letters from Paul.
16.big: Regular, planned giving is part of church life, and it binds believers of different backgrounds together.
16.diff: Paul’s care for transparency (the church chooses who carries the money) is a good model for handling church funds today.

b: ‘The first day of every week’ (verse 2) is our Sunday, the day of Jesus’ resurrection (Mark 16:2). Acts 20:7 shows believers gathering ‘on the first day of the week’ to break bread. The Didache, a church manual from the late 1st or early 2nd century, says: ‘every Lord’s day gather yourselves together, and break bread’.

16.ctx: Paul’s plans later changed, which caused friction (2 Corinthians 1:15–2:4). Pentecost (Shavuot) was in late spring.
16.mean: Paul plans to come through Macedonia and perhaps spend the winter with them, ‘if the Lord permits.’ For now he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, ‘because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.’
16.big: Paul plans his travels around gospel opportunities, even in the face of opposition, and holds his plans loosely before the Lord.

16.ctx: Timothy was young and perhaps timid (1 Timothy 4:12; 2 Timothy 1:7). The Corinthians had set Apollos up as a rival to Paul.
16.mean: ‘If Timothy comes, see to it that he has nothing to fear while he is with you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, just as I am.’ ‘No one, then, should treat him with contempt.’ As for Apollos, Paul had ‘strongly urged him’ to visit, but Apollos ‘was not at all inclined to go now’.
16.big: Paul and Apollos, whom the Corinthians had set up as rivals, were in fact colleagues.

16.ctx: Five short commands that sum up the letter, written to a church that was divided, proud and careless.
16.mean: ‘Be on the alert. Stand firm in the faith. Be men of courage. Be strong. Do everything in love.’ Paul commends ‘Stephanas and his household’, the first converts in Achaia, who ‘have devoted themselves to the service of the saints’, and asks the church to follow such people. Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus had come to Paul from Corinth and ‘refreshed my spirit and yours as well.’
16.big: Courage and love belong together in Christian character.
16.diff: ‘Be men of courage’ translates one Greek word meaning ‘act like men’: be brave and mature. Paul addresses the whole church, women included. He immediately joins it to ‘Do everything in love.’ Strength without love, or love without courage, falls short.

16.ctx: Paul dictated his letters to a secretary and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark that the letter was genuine (compare Galatians 6:11; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).
16.mean: Greetings come from ‘The churches in the province of Asia’, and from ‘Aquila and Prisca… and so does the church that meets at their house.’ This couple had worked with Paul in Corinth (Acts 18:2–3). ‘Greet one another with a holy kiss.’ Then Paul takes the pen: ‘This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under a curse. Come, O Lord! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with all of you in Christ Jesus.’
16.big: The letter ends with a prayer for the Lord’s return and a final word of love.

b: Paul writes ‘Come, O Lord!’ (verse 22) in Aramaic, Marana tha, the language of the first Jewish believers in Judea and Galilee, in a Greek letter to a mostly Gentile church. The Didache includes the same prayer in its words for the Lord’s Supper: ‘Maran atha. Amen.’ The phrase shows that the very earliest Aramaic-speaking Christians were already praying to Jesus as ‘Lord’ and asking him to come. It was not a later Greek development.
